utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen; good afternoon to the technical booth, to the interpreters, to the Registry. I also greet the parties. Madam Registrar, can you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-29-PT, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ierace, can you please introduce the people who are with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. To my left I have Morris Anyah, to my left, Chester Stamp, who are members of the trial team, and Edel Guzman, the case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Madam Pilipovic, can we have the appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. The Defence of General Galic is today represented by myself, Mara Pilipovic, and my colleague, Mr. Stephane Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Good afternoon, General Galic. So we are meeting today to continue with the Pre-Trial Conference. As you know, last week we already had our agenda; however, we know that the Prosecutor promised to make an effort in order to look again at the witness list following our recommendations. We were dealing with the other issue, that of exhibits. Does the Prosecutor want to mention changes that might have an impact on our agenda? Are we going to hear the Prosecutor as to possible results or are we going to carry on with our agenda, meaning by that that we would take up our second item, so look at exhibits from the point of view of the Trial Chamber. I'd like to know what Mr. Ierace thinks about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would be grateful for the opportunity to update the pre-trial Chamber and my learned friends on progress that the Prosecution has made since last Thursday on reducing the number of witnesses overall and also in relation to 92 bis. Your Honour, at the appropriate time, I would also appreciate the opportunity to make some general observations in relation to the exhibit list which I think Your Honours will be grateful to know. They impact directly on the timetable. Your Honour, in relation to the efforts by the Prosecution since last Thursday, I can now indicate that the Prosecution has deleted from the list of 217 witnesses, 29 witnesses. In addition to that, 16 witnesses who previously we proposed to call to give evidence in the proceedings, we now propose as 92 bis, that is, Rule 92 bis witnesses. If ultimately the Trial Chamber agrees to that proposal, then clearly that will be 16 witnesses who will not be required to give evidence, and therefore the time estimate in relation to them will be obviated. I also remind Your Honours that there are 22 witnesses proposed for coming under Rule 92 bis, which are yet to be ruled upon. Presumably that will happen with the Trial Chamber. In relation to those original 22 92 bis witnesses, the time estimate for the Prosecution case, which was contained in the filing documents for the 65 ter summaries, included those 22 92 bis witnesses. In other words, that original time estimate has to be clarified downwards if those 22 witnesses are accepted as 92 bis witnesses. Your Honours, the estimate also now has to be adjusted downwards in order to accommodate the observations made by this pre-trial Chamber last Thursday in relation to expert witnesses. For example, one of those experts was marked down for ten hours in the 65 ter summary, that being Rick Butler. So in relation to that witness alone, the estimate comes down by ten hours, given that now his report can be tendered and that will be his evidence in chief. Additionally, there are seven witnesses in respect of whom there have been discussions between the Defence and the Prosecution as to who -- as to which party should call them. Those witnesses are Colonel Zarkovic, Major General Lugonja, Major General Sladoje, Milenko Indic, Major General Lizdek, and Kovacevic. I will have some discussions with the Defence in due course as to which party should call those witnesses. I understand from early discussions that my friend would prefer that she call them. Your Honours, that is the update in relation to witnesses. I am grateful for the additional time which we have been afforded to further refine the list. It may be that in the course of the next few weeks there are some further deletions as we examine the list and the need to call each of those witnesses. Would this be a convenient time for me to make some observations in relation to the exhibit list?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but Mr. Ierace, we might possibly deal with this first, and we will deal with the exhibit list later on. I might give you the floor later on, but in relation to each question, and then you may make your comments, if you don't mind. Let's take up the second item on the agenda, as established for this Pre-Trial Conference, and this was precisely that of the exhibits. There may be a need, Mr. Prosecutor, for changes to be made, especially if, as you pointed out, you changed the number of exhibits. Initially when we started this Pre-Trial Conference, the Prosecutor had submitted a list of 5.107 exhibits, of which 4.978 had been dated and ordered in -- chronologically ordered from 1984 to 2001. The exhibits aimed at giving a detailed description of events in Bosnia before, during, and after the siege of Sarajevo. It is possible to order the exhibits in ten main categories. This is a way of organising them, and parties, of course, may have either criteria that they rely upon, but we use these criteria, and I suggest we use them to start with. A first category was that of communications between international authorities. There are many exhibits falling under this category. The second category, that of communications between Serb authorities; third category, communications between Serb and international authorities, including minutes of meetings; fourth category, press clippings and video footage; fifth category, circulars and military regulations; sixth category, witness statements; seventh category, medical Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. reports; eighth category, expert reports: military, population, ballistics, and any other expert reports already mentioned at our last meeting; ninth category, Prosecutor's exhibits. What do we mean by that? We mean those exhibits as prepared by the Prosecutor or coming from the Prosecutor, for instance, photographs, maps, letters, et cetera. And there is another category reserved for anything not falling under the other nine categories already mentioned, so that would be miscellaneous, as it were. The exhibits only have meaning if they are examined in their context, in their background, so it is necessary to specify the type of the exhibits submitted by the Prosecutor for his case, depending on the dates of the exhibits. The first exhibits date back to 1984, 1988, and 1990, The circulars and military regulations applicable in Yugoslavia. Those dating back to 1991 deal with the political background in Bosnia, and more specifically, in Sarajevo. Exhibits dating back to 1992 deal, generally speaking, with the military situation in the area of Sarajevo. Many exhibits are telegrammes exchanged between international military authorities and Serb military authorities, or else there are reports made by international military people to their superiors regarding the military situation prevailing around Sarajevo, as well as the consequences of the armed conflict on the inhabitants of the area of Sarajevo. Those of 1993 keep referring to the military situation, to the political situation too, in Sarajevo and around Sarajevo, on a daily basis. Some of them are exchanges between Serb and international authorities or else between international authorities. They also are minutes of meetings on attempted negotiations by international authorities towards ceasefire agreements. The exhibits dated 1994 are similar to those from 1993. Some of them are military reports on the military situation in Bosnia and in Sarajevo, whilst others are press clippings or footage showing the political and military situation in Central Bosnia; others show civilian casualties and a limited number of exhibits refer to General Galic. Exhibits dated 1995 contain medical reports regarding the victims of the siege of Sarajevo and reports mentioning information related to the Sarajevo siege. Exhibits of 1996 include a lot of photographs, including photographs showing the positions of marksmen during the siege of Sarajevo, as well as graveyard locations; others concern the accused directly. Some of the exhibits dated 1997 and 1998 are also documents mentioning the promotion received by General Galic, and other exhibits of the year 1997 are medical reports regarding the victims of the conflict from 1992 to 1995. The exhibits for the year 1999 mention damage inflicted during the conflict, the 1992 to 1995 conflict. Those exhibits of the year 2000 are Prosecutor's letters, and the exhibits dated 2001 are photographs. There are also many exhibits that are not dated. Generally speaking, they are medical reports, or medical documents, witness statements, military reports, reports on orders for various types of equipment necessary, further conduct of the conflict. There are expert reports, combat orders, and film footage. Let us mention four types of comments. The Chamber notes that the number of exhibits that the Prosecutor intends to submit is very large. The Chamber wonders if something cannot be done in order not to have such a flood of documents. Looking at the exhibit lists, one can see that a large number of exhibits do not have a direct bearing on the charges against General Galic but that instead they make it possible to establish the political and military background, context of Bosnia during the siege of Sarajevo. Once it has been established that the siege of Sarajevo took place in the framework of an armed conflict, would it not be suitable for the Prosecutor to only adduce, or submit, rather, those exhibits that have a direct bearing on the part played by General Galic in the events of the Sarajevo siege? Let me take an example. If you want to determine whether General Galic is guilty or not, is it necessary to know that during the siege of Sarajevo, there were conflicts between the Croat and Serbs forces or that the attack on Srebrenica was being prepared? Generally speaking, should we not try to aim at some kind of equilibrium, balance, between the number and types of witnesses and the type and number of exhibits? So this is my very first question, Mr. Prosecutor. Maybe we can get a first reaction from you. We've got another three comments to make, but to make your life easier, maybe you might want to respond to this first comment already now. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Indeed, Your Honour, since last Thursday, the Prosecution has reduced the number of entries on the exhibit list from 5.108 to approximately 3.180. That process was partly facilitated by the filing by the Defence of its pre-trial brief which for the first time made clear to the Prosecution what was and was not in dispute. The Prosecution has removed from the exhibit list the documents which on the version filed are described as unsourced. Those documents related in a large part to events elsewhere in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The relevance of those documents in part was to demonstrate the significance from the perspective of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps and it's leadership of maintaining engagement with the forces of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It's now apparent from the content of the Defence pre-trial brief that an explicit objective of the forces under the command of General Galic was to retain, was to keep, pin down, so to speak, the 75.000 troops of the Bosnia-Herzegovina government. The list has also had taken from it a number of articles which were published in the local Sarajevan newspaper, Oslobodjenje. They have been removed. So together, those documents constitute 1.103 entries, which have been taken out. There have been a number of other documents also removed, following the opportunity we had for further perusal and again in particular, in light of the Defence pre-trial brief. I would like to make some observations at this point in relation to the balance of the document. Your Honours will note that occasionally Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. there is a reference to a collection of documents rather than one particular document. An example of that in the filed exhibit list is item 5068 which is described as "Over 2.000 documents received from the Defence pursuant to Rule 67." Although that collection numbers some 2.000 documents, they are listed as one entry, because the Prosecution has not yet had the opportunity to sift through those documents and determine which, if any, will be exhibits in the Prosecution case. The reason for that lack of opportunity is two reasons. Firstly, the backlog with the Translation Unit. The documents are either still waiting to be translated or have just been translated. And secondly, that the flow of documents continues to come, and I don't mean that by way of criticism of the Defence. Your Honours, translation of the items on the exhibit list does continue to be a problem for us. A recent judgement in the case of Tuta Stela made clear that there must be translations of exhibits available, certainly by the time that they are tendered if not by the time that they are entered on the exhibit list at this stage. It's, I think, widely known and understood within the Tribunal that, for whatever reason, at the moment the Translation Unit has more work than it can handle, and thus all parties - the Prosecution, the Defence, and even the Trial Chamber - is experiencing extreme difficulties in having this work translated. Since the exhibit list has been so drastically reduced from the version which was filed on the 1st of November, it's not possible for me at this stage to indicate with precision how many documents on it await translation, but I can assist the Trial Chamber with some approximate figures. Documents and videos and the like, which require translation from B/C/S to English, number approximately 2.100; from English to B/C/S, there are approximately 1200 entries. I will be able to give more precise figures once we have an opportunity to assess the list following the recent major deletions from it. Our most recent inquiries from the Translation Unit indicate that the current capability of translating documents from B/C/S to English is around 10 to 15 documents per week. Clearly that rate is unacceptable from the perspective of this trial, which is due to commence on the 3rd of December. One hopes that if we carefully prioritise the items on the exhibit list, that at least we will achieve the position whereby when we tender an item, it has been translated and the translation has been disclosed, hopefully some weeks before that point. Your Honours, by way of assistance in relation to the -- some other issues, I should say, to do with the exhibit list, the Prosecution still has to disclose some items which are on the exhibit list. That situation comes about because ultimately of the sheer size of this case, the Prosecution resources have been in a large part, if not primarily, directed towards meeting its reciprocal disclosure obligations, and I remind Your Honours of the statistics which I gave at the last Status Conference in that regard, the sheer enormity of that task. Therefore, it happens that having finished project X, as it was known, there still remain a large number of items which are to be disclosed. The best estimate I can give as to when that will be achieved by is by the end of the month. That is assuming that the documents are burned on to CDs and those CDs are made available to the Defence. There are approximately, and this is only an estimate, some 1900 entries to be disclosed. I will be able to give a more accurate estimate again once we have collated the list following the reduction on it by 2.000 entries. Your Honours have mentioned -- Your Honour has mentioned the number of items in the list which could be described as military communications to various parties. There are some 531 documents described as UNMO documents, that is, documents generated by the UN Military Observers and some 460 documents generated by UNPROFOR. That gives one a total of some 1.000 such documents. The Prosecution intends to call some analysts who will provide in due course an expert report in relation to that material. I mention that at this stage so as to give some comfort both to Your Honours and to the Defence that in due course they will receive a report which will in effect distil the contents of those documents into a more readily accessible form of information and evidence. In other words, someone will go through those various documents and distil from them the propositions which in the Prosecution case are significant. I say that at this stage to avoid the Defence, if it so chooses, to save the time it would spend in going through them one by one and perhaps await the reports which will make clear what is relevant and what is not relevant from them. I also note that of the 3.180 entries which the second version of the exhibit list will contain, that accounts for one-third. Your Honour, as to when the Prosecution will be able to file the revised exhibit list, my best estimate is Thursday, that's the 15th of November. We're in the process at the moment, having broken it down to sections which have been processed by various members of the team, of reassembling it, and I anticipate that will be done by Thursday or Friday of this week. Your Honour, finally, I wish to make this observation: Last Thursday Your Honour asked me if I thought that an adjournment of these proceedings was appropriate in view of the Defence application that the proceedings should be adjourned pending the Appeals Chamber deciding whether it would give leave to appeal to the Defence. My response was that the Prosecution took the view it was not appropriate to adjourn for that purpose. It was open to this Chamber to consider its position once the Appeals Chamber has ruled on the question of leave to appeal. However, having said that, as Your Honours will have observed from the progress that has been made by the Prosecution in the last four days in terms of further refining the Prosecution case, in a significant way, to make it more easily understood by both the pre-trial Chamber and the Defence, it follows that if there is an adjournment of some weeks, that time will ultimately quiet clearly produce a more smoothly running and shorter Prosecution case, and it will also produce a case which is more easily understood by the Defence; in other words, it will impact on their ability to assimilate the material with which they are being presented. Your Honours will be aware that the Prosecution, and indeed the Prosecution together with the Defence, indicated some four or five weeks ago that if the trial was to commence on or about the 9th of January, both Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. sides were confident that they would be ready. Your Honours, the response from the pre-trial Chamber, having considered carefully that proposal, was to require us to be ready by the 3rd of December, and we will be ready by the 3rd of December to open, to call our witnesses. There will, however, be the discomfort of late disclosure of some aspects of the exhibit list and the late availability of translations of exhibit list items. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe you have covered our comments and remarks. I had told you that we had basically four comments to make. So I'm not going to add more comments right now. I'm going to take up what you said. Mr. Ierace, you mentioned a reduction in the number the exhibits, moving from 5.180 to 3.180. So my first question will be this: How many documents, how many witness statements, as far as you can assess, do you have in that figure of 3.180? Because we said that there was one category, namely, those witness statements that were in the list of exhibits. So how many, approximately, documents of that type do you still have in that figure of 3.180 exhibits?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could formulate my question differently. Of course, if you have an answer, I'll take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I've conferred with my friends at the bar table. I'm not aware that there are any witness statements in the exhibit list except for a few 92 bis type witness statements, and I think there are only one or two of those. It was not my intention to place the statements of witnesses that the Prosecution proposed to call in the exhibit list; however, I suspect, on reflection, that I understand why Your Honour has that understanding. Where a witness has attached to their statement photographs, maps, and so on, then those items have been placed on the exhibit list, because in due course, they of course will be tendered by the Prosecution. If there is a reference to a witness statement in the description, then I should explain that the entry does not refer to the statement itself, only the annexes to the statement. Your Honour, whilst I'm on my feet, Your Honour has given ten categories, and I should of course say that if the pre-trial Chamber wishes the entries on the exhibit list to be placed into ten such categories, then one must allow for the necessary time to do that. Perhaps one approach would be for us to file the revised exhibit list and then in due course prepare ten lists of the contents of exhibit lists under those headings. If Your Honours thought that that would assist the Trial Chamber in coming to terms with the contents. There may be an alternative way of achieving the same objective, in other words, of categorising the entries so as to make the exhibit list as a whole more manageable and understandable, and perhaps Your Honours would allow me at some convenient time a short adjournment so I can confer with my fellows and perhaps develop a proposal for Your Honours' further consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So what you've just said, Mr. Ierace, gives rise to two comments. First comment: We used these 10 categories just for the sake of our analysis. You do not need to restructure, reorganise your exhibit list on the basis of the ten categories outlined. You can structure the list as you wish, depending on your case. Second comment: You know it is the practice in many cases to ask for witness prior statements to be admitted into evidence, be they Defence or Prosecution witnesses. As we experienced it in our cases, we do not think it is necessary to proceed in that way, but it is possible for parties to use all witness prior statements made to the OTP or to Bosnian authorities. Parties can use those statements to clear up a possible contradiction arising from examination and cross-examination more generally in the testimony of a witness, to test credibility. Parties can use them. But they do not need to apply for the admission of those statements, because if you, say, use part of a witness statement, automatically that is going to be mentioned in the transcript. So there is no need to tender the whole statement. It's going to just give us more work here in the courtroom. It's more work for the registrar, because they need to have a long list of documents; it's more space in the archives, you know, that sort of thing. So think about this. Think of this suggestion made by the Chamber. Parties can use witness statements for their own sake, but they do not need to seek their admission. So this is just a suggestion I make to you. Second thing, dealing with translation problems, as you mentioned them. I do understand the whole issue of translation, but let's be creative, of course, without prejudice to the rights of the accused, without prejudice to the fairness of our trials. We do have to seek the most efficient and effective solution. And I'm going to make a suggestion to you which we have tested already in other cases. Let us imagine that the Prosecutor serves the Defence with a book of, say, 200 pages. This is nothing but an example, of course. So for his case, the Prosecutor is only going to use two or three pages out of the 200. The book is relevant, of course, for the Prosecution case, but only as far as a couple of pages are concerned. So is it absolutely necessary to have the whole book translated? And this applies also to any major document. If the Prosecution has a document of several hundred pages. And what I say to the Prosecutor applies to the Defence, of course. It goes without saying. If the Defence wants to serve the Prosecution with a book but there are only two or three relevant pages in it, I really believe we can avoid having the whole book translated. How shall we go about it? Well, the party using these couple of pages will need to send the document to the party, the other party, so that it prepare itself for the cross-examination, but will specify that only two or three pages will be used for the cross-examination of the witness or for the examination-in-chief. You know that the Prosecutor could receive a document from the Defence in B/C/S. As far as I know, the Prosecutor does have a lot of people working in his office who do speak B/C/S very well and who would be in a position to translate those couple of pages. And if the party says, "I'm going to use two or three pages but I need to know the context they find themselves in," no problem. You just turn to that person who speaks B/C/S and ask for the context. Same for the Prosecutor, who sends a document in English to the Defence. There's one thing you know. Defence Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. counsel are in exceptional circumstances authorised to represent an accused, only exceptionally, if they do not speak B/C/S or one of the official languages of the Tribunal. But if that be the case, the counsel needs to have a co-counsel who necessarily will speak one of the languages of the Tribunal. So the same could apply. In other words, if you were to receive a document in English, and it being specified that only two or three pages are going to be used, and if you are concerned to know what context those two pages are in, there is bound to be in the Defence team a person who reads or understands one of the languages used in the Tribunal. That person can therefore translate for the purpose of a cross-examination those pages and establish the context as well. Take B/C/S or English, depending, put the version on the ELMO in the courtroom, and you've got interpreters in the courtroom as well, and they will straight away translate the text. Even for the accused, for everybody present in the courtroom. And to be of further assistance when it comes to translation, when you do serve the document, you could also give it to the interpreting booth so that the interpreters can have the text on paper. But one thing is certain: Interpreters will always have the text in front of them, on the ELMO, for instance. So please be aware of this. I think one thing is not negotiable. One thing is certain. The accused must be provided with all the documents that were at the basis that were used to draft the indictment. Anything else is negotiable. You mentioned the Martinovic/Naletilic decision, Mr. Ierace, indeed. But of course given this reality parties can operate, but of course without prejudice to the rights of the accused and to the fairness of the trial, it is necessary to do it that way. I don't think there is any major prejudice, because the Rule would apply to both parties equally, and we know that counsel can very well handle the situation. If the document is a long one, but only some pages of it will be used, it is possible for both parties to prepare themselves from either the examination-in-chief or the cross-examination. So we were talking about 3.300 documents that have to be translated for the Prosecutor. If you go along with what I've just suggested - and I keep emphasising that it must be fair for both parties - if you could agree as to the way of proceeding, you will release a lot of resources and will save a lot of resources if you were in a position to agree on this position. I do not think it is fair to impose on the International Community that we all represent here, it is not fair to impose on it an additional cost that we could reasonably avoid. I'll give you the floor, Mr. Ierace, and I'll give the floor to the Defence counsel as well, so that you can react to what I've just suggested, and which has been tested in other cases. Of course, the last straw was to interrupt the trial, because we had to wait for a translation, but we should not just remain in the realm of theory. We should be more practical and cooperate. And I can sense from the outset in this case that there is a fair degree of cooperation between the parties, and we've got to remain in this good spirit to proceed accordingly. Of course, if there was a problem, a break, of course that would be serious, but it's not the case. Sorry for repeating myself, but I think that we reached a situation where the situation is either to go along with my suggestion and would be to proceed whilst being fair to the accused and to the trial, or else we'll never reach the deadline. So Mr. Ierace, what is your view on this, to solve the problems of translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Your Honour has proposed various ways in which the lack of translation facilities could be overcome. I'm aware that some of those ways have been employed in other cases, and the Prosecution has no difficulty with utilising those various methods. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Pilipovic. I see. It's Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to respond to the principle, but first of all I wish to thank this Tribunal most warmly for the effort made to reorganise, in a sense, and restructure this list of witnesses, and I'm all the more grateful as the task is not an easy one. I also wish to thank the Prosecution for the considerable effort they have invested, and if I understood correctly the current state of affairs, they still don't know which exhibits have a probative value and which do not, and we are told that after some two years. But we have to be practical, and our reaction is exactly the same as that of the Chamber. How we can simplify and economise on the resources of the International Community by not doing things that are completely useless. Let us systemise things first. First we have PC material. I hope I will not be misunderstood, but anyway, a whole pile of documents, and I think that the two don't cohabit. They should be separated. And I would suggest that we see whether the Prosecutor can produce a very simple document. I'm talking about this O21, 0010108 and 00CL [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, that the numerical references have not appeared correctly on the transcript, so would you please check. I think there's some confusion there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. I don't quite understand what you mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the numbers that you mentioned of the disks did not appear on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does that mean that we can't work on them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It just means that you should repeat the numbers, if you could.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, excuse me. Yes. Of the disk that we received from the Prosecution on the 2nd of October has the number 0210010A, and I have it in my hands. And also GPX00CL.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those are the two CDs. Allow me to interrupt you. Perhaps you could make that suggestion directly to the Prosecution, because the Chamber doesn't have those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would be glad to provide the Chamber with copies, Mr. President. It's rather important to show us to what extent the task is difficult for the Defence and then we will address the question of translation, if necessary. Perhaps I could give the Madam Registrar or someone else what exhibit I am referring to which is one in so many others. Who should I give it to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the Registry. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll be glad to do that. I have some consternation, Mr. President, because I really do not see in a Tribunal of this importance, when all of us wish to save the funds of the International Community, what is the weight of such an exhibit? And before I address the question of translation, I think that we must, much more systematically, select all these exhibits and speak about them only then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, your suggestion is a reasonable one, but I don't know whether this is the right moment to raise it. Maybe there's another way of doing it, and I should like to make a suggestion to you. For the moment, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you have I think to bear two things in mind. The first is: What is your opinion regarding the suggestion I made regarding the practical way of overcoming the problems of translation? And the other point: If the Defence is already in a position to tell us which are the exhibits whose authenticity they contest. Before giving you the floor, let me say something else. As you know, Rule 65 ter makes it incumbent upon the Prosecutor to file its pre-trial brief together with a list of witnesses, a list of exhibits. It is true that the Prosecutor filed its pre-trial brief without a list of witnesses and without a list of exhibits, which put the Defence in the situation you described last week. That is, you had little time to read the list of witnesses and the list of exhibits. But the position of the Chamber is identical to that of the Defence, because we received it at the same time as you. We know one thing now, and that is a point that needs to be considered and which I wish to address with you, and that is linked to the question of the adjournment of the trial or not to wait for the ruling on the appeal of the Defence, and that is that we are quite convinced that it is not possible, and I would say permissible, for this pre-trial stage to last two years, and we clearly have to begin this trial as soon as possible. Because if we don't begin, the date that I gave you, then the trial -- we might need a lot of time to find the next trial date, and this is not due to less -- lack of diligence on the part of the Chamber that the trial has not started. It is not the responsibility of the Chamber. But what is the responsibility of the Chamber is to do everything, and I must apologise for the authoritarian way I have adopted by saying we are going to open this trial, even if the parties request more time. Therefore, the position of the Chamber is that we're going to leave this case in a condition ready for beginning of trial. As for the appeals ruling, that is something additional to the heart of the matter, and then the Trial Chamber can easily accept the ruling and start again. But there is still work to be done before the beginning of trial. The parties are not just going to sit around and wait until the date comes for the beginning of trial. They have to continue working and preparing, and even then, of course, they will not have finished their work. They will have to continue working. You know very well that even after a trial begins, the preparatory work which is ongoing continues right through until the end. So Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I understand your suggestion, but I think that this work of triage, of selection of documents, is a job that the Defence can begin to do in order to achieve the first objective, that is, to see which documents can -- on which translation can be saved. Then the second group is the group of documents whose authenticity is contested by the Defence. Because these are two really important aspects for organising this chapter of exhibits. And as I am saying, this can be done directly between the parties, because after all, the Chamber only has a list of the exhibits, not the exhibits themselves. So I must say, with all due respect, that it would be a waste of time for the Chamber to analyse each and every exhibit. We just have the list. After that, for the Trial Chamber, yes, they can look at the documents themselves. But to have those documents, we need to organise them first, because otherwise -- I'm sorry for saying this, but if there are so many documents that the Prosecutor has given to the Defence and should be thrown into the wastepaper basket, and the other way around, we have to make a selection, otherwise we will be throwing a lot into the wastepaper basket. So the practical suggestion I have made goes a bit beyond the question of translation. That is one question. And the other is whether you may be able, perhaps in two or three weeks, to communicate to us which of the exhibits whose authenticity you are contesting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I want to thank you once again, Mr. President, because we can agree with you on many points, first of all on the need to be rigorous and to reorganise things properly. Ms. Pilipovic will react to the second point. As to the first point, personally speaking, because I am personally involved in this, I think that your suggestion in principle is an interesting one. Why is it interesting? For many reasons, but let me first mention two things. Firstly, that, as you reminded us, there is the absolute rights for the accused to have access to essential documents in a language that he understands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry for interrupting you. You mean essential documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I agree with you. What I mean is that in part today some of these documents have not yet been provided to the accused. I stop here for the first point. And as to the second, unfortunately so, I gave you this document as a bit of a humorous thing, but it is not humorous at all, as long as the Defence do not know exactly what is on this hard disk, on this CD. If there are a couple of examples like this one, which I am a bit ashamed to show you, but I didn't produce them, I'm not in a position to tell you what the state of affairs is as long as the Prosecution has not sorted things properly. It is unacceptable. It is nearly reprehensible. I was going to say that, but I'll withdraw that. It is not acceptable for documents to be produced whilst they've only been produced through automatic scanning, because if it was not the case it would be even more serious. Ms. Pilipovic is going to meet the second point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I understand that you expect an answer from me to your second question regarding the revision of the exhibit list of the Prosecution. As far as I have been able to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. understand, the Prosecution, my learned friends, believe that it would be sufficient for them to have two or three weeks to revise those documents, review those documents, upon which the Defence would be served with that document, and then the Defence would have to state whether it contests the authenticity of those documents or not. I expect that you will give my learned friends opposite sufficient time and that the Defence, pursuant to Rule 65 ter, will be served and will be able to respond regarding those whose authenticity we contest. In that situation, it would be possible for the Trial Chamber to be as effective and efficient as possible. Of course, that decision is in your hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Madam Pilipovic. There were some other observations I wanted to make. I think that we are now in a situation when there is an enormous risk of repetitiveness of documents. There was an exchange of documents. Documents have been communicated by the Prosecution to the Defence, and vice versa. What may happen is that there's a duplication of documents, and we may find ourselves in a situation of having an exhibit with one particular exhibit number and the same exhibit with a different exhibit number, and I think this effort of reorganisation must take care to identify a repetition of documents, that is, the same document bearing different numbers. Again, we will have to throw them into the wastepaper basket, and we are in that way too risking wasting energy and effort. What I think that we should do, and we always did in our Chamber, is, after having selected all those documents and after having an indication from the Defence which of the documents they contest, we could organise a complete file of Prosecution exhibits which would be marked for identification by the Registry. For now it would be the Prosecution exhibits. After that it will be the Defence exhibits. And the Registry would mark those exhibits so that when a party is presenting its case, it will say, "I now wish to discuss document which has such-and-such a number," and then immediately the other party and the Judges know which document is being referred to and there is no need only then to pick up the document, ask the usher to show it to the Registry, for the Registry to mark it for identification, to distribute it in the courtroom, et cetera, et cetera. This is not a tailorist version of work, but certainly a way of saving time, and the parties will have more time to prepare because they will have a whole file containing all the exhibits, with all the appropriate numbers, before them, those that are not contested. And then the Chamber might already rule on their admission. But I don't think we are really working under a system in which documents could be admitted, no. The system might allow it, because, as you know, the Tribunal system regarding the admission of documents is not strictly common law; that is, all the documents need to be verified, because the documents will be -- are not going to be submitted to a jury who are non-professional here. It is the Judges that decide. And that is why as soon as the question of authenticity has been overcome, there is nothing further to do regarding admission, because the Judges from the holisitc point of view, which is to say that all of the documents have to be seen in their integrity and it is up to the Judges to judge their probative value, and since that is so, there's no point in discussing their admissibility. What I consider to be important is to know what is the position of the Defence, or the other way around. During the Defence case the Prosecution position regarding authenticity. As soon as authenticity is not contested, the document could automatically be admitted into evidence. I think I have lost from sight another matter that I wish to draw your attention to, and that is avoiding duplication of documents either on the side of the Prosecution or the document that may have been received by the Prosecution from the Defence. A third point that I wish to share with you is the question of the Prosecution has told us that they have some other documents to communicate to the Defence, and I think that all these matters need to be borne in mind for future communication. That is, ongoing communicating, duplicate, is this document really important? could I first discuss it with the Defence to see whether the document can be served without waiting for the translation unless it is really a crucial document for the case. I think there are documents that are of essential importance, and in that case the matter cannot be negotiated. But there is a whole pile of other documents that are quite peripheral regarding the actual key of the case, and in this area I think there is a large field of cooperation between the two parties. I find it most commendable, and I think we should highlight that too, that Mr. Prosecutor, you have made a list of documents, linked them together, so that we have a view of the whole. I think it is also important to speak with the Defence, because maybe the Defence -- I think mention has been made of an analyst, which is close to an expert witness, but we stick to the term "analyst." The Defence may also wish to have an analyst in order perhaps to respond. When we're dealing with expert witnesses. And the other party needs to respond through the cross-examination, we have permitted the presence of an expert witness in the courtroom who does not take the floor but who can give suggestions for the cross-examination. This applies to the Prosecution case and also when the Defence case's turn comes. This expert will not take the floor but just make suggestions for the cross-examination, and I think this is always possible. And if we can save time, if we can proceed quickly, at least in this Chamber that was our practice, and maybe the Chamber which will take over will accept this procedure. To summarise all this, let me say two things: I think that what we should do, and what is reasonable to do, is to take the trial date and to make a timetable for the different stages of the preparation of the case, because of course that will not be over when the trial begins. It goes on after that. But still, there are things that we can do. So we're going to fix a date for the Prosecution to present a revised list of exhibits, taking into account all the small suggestions we have made here, that is, make a selection, indicate the essential documents, which means the documents that need to be translated, because if you give priorities to the translation section and if you ask them for a few things, you will get it from them. But if you ask the Translation Service to translate everything, you will not get the essential documents, nor the others. And also perhaps allow the Defence to respond and to express its position Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. regarding the authenticity of documents. As soon as we have that document, with the cooperation of the Registry, we perhaps will be able to mark all those documents for identification. The files could be distributed to the Defence and the Judges of the Chamber so as to have a common code of communication, if I can call it that. As soon as a document is mentioned, we know which document we're talking about. Another point is that in my opinion, we will not consider adjourning the proceedings. We will do everything so that the trial can open on the date envisaged, and taking into account this idea of continuous preparation, it is in the interests of justice and also in the interests of the rights of the accused that the trial begin under the best conditions. As you know, and as I have already said, there are elements that can be presented at the beginning of the case, and after that we will have a long break. So it's always possible to make up for lost time in the meantime. If we lose this chance of December 3rd, we may have to wait a year or longer, and that I would not like to put the Chamber that will take over in a difficult situation. I want you to understand that well. I would like to complete my mandate with completing the preparation of the case for the opening of the trial, but, of course, under the best possible conditions. We must bear in mind that the first days of this case will be opening statements, very generalised matters, so we will not enter into the case during the first few days. So we'll have more time after that, and along these lines of continuous preparation, I think this is quite feasible. I think I have covered, more or less, the points I wish to address, but in my notes I see there's another point. I would like the parties to consider what we said regarding the translation of documents, and I think this could also apply to the expert reports. That was the Rule we applied in one of our cases in which the expert reports -- only the conclusions of those reports were translated. Because there's often little sense in translating thousands of pages of text when we know that it is the conclusions of the experts that are important. And I would like the parties to consider this possibility. Do we really need to have translated all the reports in their entirety, or would it be possible for us to have only the conclusions translated? That is a question I leave with you, with the added information that this is what we did in another case, because the parties agreed and the suggestion was accepted. And once again, this is a way of speeding things up and saving resources. There may be some other suggestions which I would like to make, but I think that in the decision that we will render in writing, I may make an annex of the suggestions of this Chamber which are the result of experience and which I would like to submit to the parties so that they might think them over and discuss them, but the decision regarding those suggestions would be left to the Trial Chamber. That is to say that if the parties agree with a particular suggestion, you can convey that to the Trial Chamber and tell them that the previous Chamber made this suggestion and we agree with the first, second, and third of those suggestions, or you can say that you don't agree and that you don't accept the others, for instance, the other suggestions, and then the Chamber will take whatever position it deems fit. But just to give you an example of what such a suggestion may be, I think that for the good conduct of the case, one should have a small rule, and that is that the cross-examination cannot, except exceptionally, exceed the time of the examination-in-chief. I think this can be a good rule, and this can apply to both parties; that is, when the Prosecution conducts its examination-in-chief, the Defence will have an equal amount of time for the cross-examination, but also this applies the other way around. The Prosecution will be limited in its cross-examination during the Defence case. To give you another example, there are so many questions raised in connection with protective measures. Today it is the turn of the Prosecution; tomorrow it will be the Defence. Very often, the parties require closed session, for instance, and we realise that protective measures should be coordinated with the right of the accused to have a public hearing and at the same time to protect the victims. So I think there's no point in asking for a closed session if a witness is given a pseudonym, facial distortion, and voice distortion, whereby the witness is protected while at the same time the public in the gallery can hear the testimony. Because, as you know, closed session does not allow the public in the public gallery to hear the testimony. And we can use this method, I would say, to establish a balance between the right of the accused to a public hearing and the right of the victims to protection, and I think that the parties should abstain from requesting closed session hearings if a pseudonym is attributed, voice distortion and facial distortion is given, because thereby the public character of the hearing is preserved. The public can follow and hear the witness. That is simply to give you these two examples. I use those two as examples to give you an idea of some very practical suggestions that we extracted from our experience and which we should like to leave with you for your consideration and for your mutual discussions. If you agree, you will let the Trial Chamber know; if not, also the same applies. I think now I have covered all the observations I wish it make, and so we will come to the third point, and that is other matters which the parties wish to raise, any matters that you had in mind before and anything that may have cropped up today. Mr. Prosecutor, do you have any additional matters to address?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Your Honour has indicated that you propose to set a timetable for the further tasks to be done, and that will include the further disclosure of items on the exhibit list. The effect -- the inquiries which the Prosecution has made as to when that can be done by way of a compact disk suggests the end of the month, and that's assuming that all of the intermediate steps occur without any unforeseen difficulties. So far as filing the amended list of exhibits is concerned, as I've earlier said, I expect that we can comply with that certainly by the end of the week. Your Honour mentioned duplication of some of the items. The Prosecution took advantage of the last few days to check the exhibit list for duplications, and some were discovered and were eliminated. My friend on the other side has handed to Your Honour two pages which he says were Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. printed from the contents of a compact disk that was handed to the Defence by the Prosecution on the 2nd of October. That compact disk did not relate to the exhibit list. It contained documents which the Prosecution made available by way of reciprocal disclosure. I am somewhat mystified by the two documents which have been handed over, because they appear on their face to have no relevance to the Defence case, which is the purpose of reciprocal disclosure; and secondly, and more curiously, they don't contain ERN numbers. So far as I am aware, all material which the Prosecution makes -- which the Prosecution discloses to the Defence contains an ERN number. While Your Honour has been talking, we have obtained a copy of the compact disk in question and we're checking it. I would be very grateful if my friend make available the ERN numbers for those two documents or clarify if whether the follow copies are blow-ups of the page or give us any further information so we can locate where they were taken from on the compact disk Your Honour, finally, if this be the last opportunity for us to appear before you and your fellow Judges, Judge Riad and Judge Wald, I would like to convey on behalf of the Prosecution in the case of Galic our gratitude and thanks for your assistance and the assistance of your fellow Judges in readying this case for trial. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Ierace. The information that you have requested of the Defence, I think that the Defence can provide you with that information after the hearing. Any additional matters before we adjourn, Ms. Pilipovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that we have had a very fruitful hearing today, but the Defence wishes to raise a few more matters which we believe to be very important for the purposes of this case. First of all, the Defence would like to have the Chamber's permission to call all of the witnesses with whom the Prosecution has had interviews, that is, the witnesses who were members of the Sarajevo Romanija corps, the witnesses in respect of whom my learned colleague has already notified the Chamber, the witnesses whose statements we are dealing with here. Those witnesses have been interviewed by the OTP, and they include five members, ex-members of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, and the Defence should like the Chamber to give the permission to call them as their witnesses should the Prosecutor decide not to call them, as well as other witnesses with whom the Prosecutor has had interviews but has not included them in the witness list. The second matter which we wish to address before the Chamber is the issue of Prosecutor's pre-trial brief and unscheduled sniping incidents and witnesses relating to those incidents. We should like to hear the Prosecutor as to the meaning of scheduled and unscheduled incidents. What is it that the Prosecution means by that? So as to make it possible for the Defence to prepare themselves and so that General Galic can be given a fair trial. And the third matter which we would like to raise before the Chamber and in respect of which we expect a decision by the Chamber: We should like an obligation to be imposed upon the parties that names of witnesses be provided to the other party eight days prior to the hearing. So we should like that obligation to be imposed on both parties, that the minimum deadline be eight days. That is, that the opposing parties should be informed of the names of witnesses eight days before the date that those witnesses are scheduled to testify. So those would be the issues that I wanted to address for the purposes of having a well-prepared trial in this case. And also at the end of my submissions, I should like to express my gratitude to this Chamber for the work that it has done on this case and also our gratitude for very useful suggestions, both for the Defence and for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if you allow me, I'd like to stress very briefly first of all what my colleague has just said, but I also wanted to draw the attention of this Trial Chamber to the technical problems that will crop up if we don't give ourselves the opportunity to have a quiet appraisal. I raised a very small issue, an incident, earlier on. There was a reason to it, and you can see that it sort of unleashes a series of micro incidents that may become, in a few weeks' time, macro non-events. What do I mean by that? Already, already, the quality of the documents which we have received from the Prosecutor is being challenged. Why? Because there is no ERN number. I mentioned just a few examples by selecting a few exhibits. There's no ERN numbers because they're just selected for the sake of it. But what's the purpose of producing exhibits if they don't have any numbers marked and they can't be found again? That's all. We've just told you, Mr. President, that everything is fine with the Prosecution. They have a technique by which they can trace back exhibits through the help of a specialised assistant, and that should eventuate by the end of the month if all goes well. And you said that maybe we would need our own assistant in order to proceed in the same manner. There may be a miracle in a couple of hours' time, but if there is not, what do we see? We might find ourselves in a position where the Defence, three days or three working days or even less before the trial begins would not have received to date the list of finally-selected exhibit after two years, and this is none of our responsibility. So therefore, how could we possibly start the trial, even if admittedly we'll have some time afterwards, whereas the Defence will not have been able to even open Prosecution documents. I seem to understand they were not all correct, on top of that. So we do plead, formally so, and repeat our application of last time, based on 65 ter (N), we ask formally of this Chamber that an additional time period be made available so that both parties can carry out their work. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We have worked somewhat longer than reasonably expected. We really tried our best to finish on time, and the interpreters have worked now for quite a while. But I think five more minutes will be enough for us to finish, and I think they will be happy if they don't have to come back after a break. So I think we should try and finish now. As regards the issue that has been brought up by Madam Pilipovic, I should like to tell you that we would really like to see the list of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Prosecution witnesses and to see it structured and reduced. And in view of such reductions, I think that we will have a reserve list of witnesses which may at some later stage be called by the Prosecutor, if necessary. I'm not going to say that we're not going to take into account all of the effort that has been made by the Prosecutor to reduce the list of witnesses. But, Madam Pilipovic, I don't know if we can respond, if we can grant your request to call all of the witnesses that have been included in the Prosecutor's list. Why? Because we are still at the Prosecution stage of the proceedings, and you will have to prepare yourself for the cross-examination of Prosecution witnesses. If there are witnesses on the Prosecution list of witnesses who are not going to be called but witnesses in respect of whom the Defence would like to call them, the witnesses that the Defence deems important for their case, well, in that case you can have -- you can prepare a list of such witnesses and we will take into consideration that request. Because you have to -- we have to have a different perspective on things as well, because the Prosecutor is not going to call -- the Prosecutor is going to call his witnesses and then the Defence will have an opportunity to call their witnesses. And during the Prosecution case, the Defence will be able, of course, to cross-examine their witnesses. And once the Defence opens its case, they will be able to call their witnesses and the Prosecutor will cross-examine Defence witnesses. I think that the Prosecutor will be glad to provide you with the response to your question regarding scheduled and unscheduled incidents. I think that you can have contact concerning that particular subject matter, and I hope that you will be able to inform the Chamber of that exchange. As regards this other matter which was mentioned by Madam Pilipovic, namely, the disclosure of a witness list eight days prior to the hearing, thank you very much for that suggestion, Madam Pilipovic. I think that we are on the same wavelength as regards this topic. That is exactly one of the suggestions that I wanted to include in our decision. There are others, of course, which are the result of our experience. For example, the lack of contact, decision, the possibility of requesting a lack of contact with witnesses who have already started their testimony. That will also be one of our suggestions. And those suggestions will concern both parties in the same way. As for the fourth issue which was raised by Mr. Piletta-Zanin, let me repeat the expression that you used, micro events which might lead to macro non-events, in particular, when it comes to the list of exhibits. I think that we can also have it the other way around. But I think that it is necessary for us to discuss and I think that the parties should try to reduce such list and to focus on the merits of the case, which can always be a topic of the exchanges between the parties, and during such an exchange the parties can perhaps agree on what they disagree, at least. Of course, we have this historical context of the case. That is something that can be agreed upon. It has already been discussed in a number of cases. And I think that you should focus your attention to the details and the facts that concern this particular case. There are a number of things that we already know, a series of elements and a series of facts that can be presented to the Chamber without necessarily calling appropriate witnesses. I'm referring to the general context of the conflict and so on and so forth. We should concentrate ourselves to the essentials of the case, that is, the responsibility of this particular accused in a story which is more or less familiar to all of us by now. So this is an effort that can be made by all of us. The Prosecutor has already tendered a number of similar documents in a number of other cases, but we have to concern ourselves with the specific responsibility of General Galic in the overall context of these events which are already familiar to all of us. Before we adjourn, I should like to give an opportunity to General Galic to take the floor. I don't know whether General Galic wishes to tell us anything regarding conditions of detention and condition of his health. General Galic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour, for the time, and I should also like to express my gratitude for this -- for the fact that I was always able to express myself before this Chamber, especially in regard to the conditions of detention. Speaking of my condition now, I must say that I have had some problems with my health recently, some examinations involving x-rays will be soon done, including a CT, and we will see what the results are. I have some minor problems with walking. As for other general conditions of my detention, they are as usual. I don't have anything in particular to say except to add -- except to say one more time that I should like to thank this particular Chamber for all of the work and the attention that it has paid to my case and my condition in particular.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, General Galic. I hope that your health will improve. I wish you all the best. Before we adjourn, I would like to say that it has been a pleasure to work with you in the preparation of this case. The pre-trial phase has had several special -- has known several special events, several special situations which we were not always able to control. But once again, I should like to express my appreciation for the cooperation that you have demonstrated in this case, the cooperation that I hope will be very useful for the future. We also have Mr. Piletta-Zanin here in this case now, and I hope that he will be able to provide you with very useful and precious help and assistance in this case. I also would like to just tell you that I will continue paying attention to what is happening with this case. I will remain in a certain way seized of this case in the future as well, and I thank you once again on behalf of Judge Wald as well, who is absent. Thank you on behalf of Judge Riad. Thank you once again, all of you, technicians, interpreters, and the person of the Registry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the Status Conference adjourned at
